card.title: Playing games
card.q: How does a button under your thumb move a world?

part.name: the controller
part.line: two sticks and eight buttons — every one a switch
part.blurb: Under every button is a switch, and a switch has two words: pressed and not pressed. The console never sees your thumbs; it reads a short row of ones and zeros, hundreds of times a second. Everything you ever do in the game arrives as that row, and as nothing else.

door.q: What happens between a thumb and a number?
A switch says one word — yes or no. Where does that lead?

part.name: the box under the television
part.line: a computer, wearing a costume
part.blurb: Take the case off and the parts are the same as in the phone and the laptop: a processor to follow instructions, memory to hold the world, a program saying what to do. The makers do not hide this — the processor’s name is printed on the box. A console is a computer whose program tells it to behave like a toy.

door.q: What is inside, and how does it follow a program?
Who keeps the box in order while it plays?

part.name: the processor
part.line: billions of instructions a second, none of them clever
part.blurb: Sixty times every second the processor runs the same round: read the controller, move the world forward one step, work out what the world now looks like, hand the picture to the screen. Each of the billions of instructions is no cleverer than “add these two numbers”. The speed is astonishing; every single instruction is dumb.

door.q: How does it decide, sixty times a second, what happens next?
What are the billions of instructions made of?
Working out what the world looks like — the trail of the thousand painters

part.name: memory
part.line: the world you move through, held in numbered cells
part.blurb: The city, your position in it, the score: all of it lives in memory, which is an enormous row of numbered cells, each holding a number. Change a cell and the world changes; the machine has no other way to be different. Cut the power and every cell forgets — which is why there is a save file, further down this trail.

door.q: How does a circuit hold the world you move through?
Where does the picture you see live?

part.name: the picture
part.line: two million lamps, each told how bright to be
part.blurb: The screen is a wall of tiny lamps, and each lamp is told, dozens of times a second, three numbers: how much red, how much green, how much blue. A frame of a game is about two million such trios, and the television is simply the machine obedient enough to display them. Nobody draws anything; numbers are obeyed.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
What holds two million lamps between the frames?

part.name: the shared world
part.line: two consoles, two copies, one truth to agree on
part.blurb: Play with someone far away and there is no single machine holding the world: there are two, each with its own copy, trading messages as fast as the wires allow. When two players grab the same object in the same instant, the copies disagree — and every trick the game’s programmers use to settle it descends from one old, hard question.

door.q: How do two machines share one world?
Two players, one world — what keeps it whole?

part.name: the save file
part.line: memory that survives the off switch
part.blurb: A save is a copy of the interesting cells, written onto a disk that does not forget when the power leaves. Switch on tomorrow and those numbers are read back into memory, and the world resumes exactly where it stopped. Nothing in the machine understands “saved game”; it is numbers copied faithfully from one kind of memory to another.

door.q: Who keeps the files, and who runs the machine?
How does anything survive the off switch?

card.bottom: Follow any part of this trail far enough down and it dissolves into switches: pressed and not pressed, high and low, 0 and 1. The trails below lead the rest of the way down; at their ends, the primers are waiting.

door.q: The choices that lead down to the gates
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Delivering food
card.q: What happens between the tap and the doorbell?

part.name: the phone
part.line: a computer that happens to fit in a pocket
part.blurb: The phone is the same machine as the console and the laptop: a processor, memory, and programs that give it its habits. The glass is a fine invisible grid of wires; where your finger lands, one row and one column cross, and the machine is told a coordinate, two numbers, and nothing more. It has never seen a finger in its life.

door.q: What does the glass understand?
What is the phone saying, and to whom?

part.name: the app
part.line: a list of instructions, written down in advance
part.blurb: The app is not a place and not a person: it is a long list of instructions, written in advance and followed without opinion. Each tap hands it one new fact, and it answers with the next instruction on the list. Doorbells, spaceships and food apps are all the same arrangement — instructions, obeyed exactly.

door.q: The list was written by a person, in words — the trail of how software is written
Who lets a hundred apps share one phone?

part.name: the restaurant’s side of the internet
part.line: a warehouse computer answering ten thousand strangers
part.blurb: Your tap becomes a small message, copied from your phone to a tower to a wire to a building full of computers: a server, a computer with no screen of its own, kept cool in a warehouse and answering ten thousand strangers at once. Your order lands in its memory like a note on a spike, and the reply (received) is copied back down the same road.

door.q: How does an order cross the wire to the warehouse?
Ten thousand strangers — how does it keep track?
Where do ten thousand strangers’ orders park, and how are they found again?

part.name: the match
part.line: facts and rules, searched for the answer
part.blurb: Which restaurant, which rider: the assignment is made by a machine walking through facts (this rider two kilometres away, that one busy, this kitchen needing twenty minutes) hunting for the combination that satisfies all the rules at once. No person weighs the offers; the search does. Some of the most useful software ever written is exactly this, and it is a way of speaking to a machine, not a kind of hardware.

door.q: Can you tell a machine only facts, and still get answers?
Who decides which order goes first?

part.name: the route
part.line: a city as a picture the machine can walk
part.blurb: To the machine the city is not streets and houses but corners joined by edges, each edge with a length. The best route is found by a recipe that contains a copy of itself: the cheapest way to a far corner is built out of cheapest ways to nearer ones, the same step applied again and again until nothing remains. The machine has no idea what a street is. It never needs one.

door.q: What happens when a task contains a copy of itself?
How does the map reach the courier’s phone?
The dot that starts the route — where does the phone know itself to be?

part.name: the courier’s phone
part.line: instructions, one word at a time
part.blurb: The courier’s phone speaks the way machines speak: one instruction at a time — left in two hundred metres, then arrive. The rider never sees the whole plan; they see the next word, and the next word is always enough. There is a whole tradition of computing built on exactly that discipline: a vocabulary of small words, each obeyed exactly, out of which anything can be composed.

door.q: Can a language be small enough to trust?
What is the phone saying to the dispatch?

part.name: one order, two riders
part.line: the bug the whole system exists to prevent
part.blurb: The dangerous moment is invisible: two couriers press accept on the same order in the same instant. Two hands, one memory cell, no agreed order — and a carelessly built system can hand one meal to two riders, or to none. Every ordering system on earth is, at bottom, a scheme for making that impossible.

door.q: What happens when two act on the same thing at once?
How does the order reach exactly one rider?
One meal, one rider, one payment — how money stays counted once

card.bottom: The phone, the app, the warehouse, the match: each is the same machine in different clothes: switches, numbers, instructions. The trails below take those words one layer at a time; at their ends stand the primers, each one alone.

door.q: The trail that ends at a real machine
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Watching movies
card.q: Where does a film live while you watch it?

part.name: the screen
part.line: two million lamps, each told what to be
part.blurb: A television picture is about two million tiny lamps, each given, dozens of times a second, three numbers: how much red, how much green, how much blue. A film is therefore a river of numbers arriving just in time to be shown, and the screen is the machine obedient enough to turn them into light. The pause button does not stop the world; it stops the numbers.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
What holds the picture between the beats?

part.name: the sound
part.line: your evening, measured 44,100 times a second
part.blurb: Sound reaches the ear as pressure in the air. A microphone measures it 44,100 times a second and writes each measurement down as a number; a speaker reads the numbers back and recreates the pressure. Music on a computer is a long column of numbers and nothing else — the screen’s trick, one dimension over.

door.q: How does a song become numbers, and back again?
Is a picture caught the same way?

part.name: the stream
part.line: a film poured through a wire, just in time
part.blurb: The numbers cannot all be sent at once, so they are poured: a few million bits a second, arriving shortly before they are needed. When more arrives than the wire can carry, the picture thins to grey blocks and a stutter, and that is the wire telling the truth about itself.

door.q: How does a film cross the wire, just in time?
Who keeps the film arriving just in time?

part.name: the buffer
part.line: the next minute of the film, parked in your living room
part.blurb: Because wires stutter, the player keeps a cushion: half a minute or so of the future, already arrived and held in memory. When the wire coughs, the film keeps playing out of the cushion, and the race between arrival and playback starts again quietly. The buffer is memory doing what memory exists to do: holding a state against time.

door.q: How does a circuit hold anything against time?
Why hold a copy until the far end answers?

part.name: the squeeze
part.line: a program that decides what your eye will not miss
part.blurb: Two million lamps repainted dozens of times a second is past what any household wire can carry, so a program called the codec compresses the numbers: this frame is nearly the last frame, this block of sky barely changes, and the eye forgives. The film you see is the codec’s opinion of the film, computed on the fly, and it is a program like any other: instructions, obeyed exactly.

door.q: What exactly is being squeezed, and what is it made of?
The codec decides — what is deciding made of?

part.name: the buttons
part.line: a language of a dozen words
part.blurb: Play. Pause. Back ten seconds. The remote’s whole vocabulary is a dozen words, and the player obeys one at a time, in the order pressed, without ever guessing. It is the oldest arrangement in computing, a small vocabulary and exact obedience, and there are whole languages built on nothing but it.

door.q: Two whole languages made of almost nothing
Every button a switch — what do switches say?

part.name: the suggestions
part.line: facts about millions of evenings, walked to a guess
part.blurb: “Because you watched” is a machine searching recorded facts (millions of evenings, what was finished, what was abandoned) for what fits yours. It is not a person and it is not magic; it is search through relations, the same craft that assigns a rider to an order, run at planetary scale.

door.q: Facts about millions of evenings, walked to a guess
Where do the facts about evenings come from?
Search is where it starts — how a machine improves its guesses
The other guesser — a machine that answers in words

card.bottom: Lamps, pressure, wires, cushions: numbers all the way down, and numbers the machine can only hold and obey. The bottom of the deck explains how anything this obedient can also be this capable.

door.q: The trail that ends at the Bit and at memory
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Forecasting the weather
card.q: Where does tomorrow's weather come from?

part.name: the observation
part.line: the whole sky, measured and rounded to numbers
part.blurb: On the hour, all round the world, the air is read: thermometers and barometers in tens of thousands of stations, balloons climbing through the cold with little boxes dangling beneath them, radar sweeping the rain, satellites photographing the clouds from above. Every instrument does the same one thing: it measures heat, pressure, wind or wetness, and rounds each measurement to a number. The sky at this hour is, to the machine, a few million numbers, and nothing else.

door.q: The air, measured and numbered, exactly like a song
How do a million readings reach the model in time?
The satellites among the observers — the trail of how they are run

part.name: the picture
part.line: tomorrow, painted from numbers
part.blurb: What reaches you is a picture: a map washed in colours, a ribbon of little hour-by-hour icons, a sun that is itself a small drawing. None of it is sent; all of it is drawn, on your phone, from the model’s numbers, by a program whose whole job is turning a column of figures into reds and blues. The sun on the forecast screen is three numbers telling a lamp how brightly to shine.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
How does the forecast cross the wire to your pocket?

part.name: the model
part.line: the laws of the air, spelled as arithmetic
part.blurb: Air is not mysterious. It obeys a short list of laws, known for two centuries: it is pushed from where the pressure is high to where it is low, warm air rises and carries its wetness with it, and steam lets go of its heat the moment it turns to rain. A weather model is those laws rewritten as arithmetic, millions of small sums, one minute of sky at a time, followed exactly, with no opinion about picnics. It is a program like any other: instructions, obeyed.

door.q: One rule, every cell, one beat — the trail of simulated worlds
A million yes-or-no forks inside one step of sky

part.name: the grid
part.line: the sky, cut into a lattice of numbered cells
part.blurb: A machine cannot hold the continuous sky, so it cuts the sky up: the globe laid out in a lattice of boxes a few kilometres wide, stacked upward in floors, each box carrying its own numbers — pressure, temperature, wind, wetness. Each minute of the forecast is every box asking its neighbours a question at once. The machine has no idea what weather is. It walks a lattice of cells, and the lattice is enough.

door.q: A picture is a grid of trios — is the sky caught the same way?
Cells, neighbours, a rule — the trail of worlds walked this way

part.name: the machine that runs it
part.line: the largest computers on earth, doing sums about rain
part.blurb: Walking millions of boxes forward, minute by minute, is the heaviest routine arithmetic in the world, and it runs on the largest machines there are: warehouses of cabinets, each cabinet the same design as the phone in your pocket, thousands of them computing one sky side by side. Nothing exotic hides inside. It is the familiar dance of fetch, decode and execute, multiplied until tomorrow fits inside an afternoon.

door.q: The stored program — the one design in every box
Thousands of boxes, one sky — the trail of many machines as one

part.name: the forty skies
part.line: the same question asked of slightly different mornings
part.blurb: The observation is honest but incomplete: a breeze missed here, a degree missed there. So the model is run not once but many times, from many slightly different first numbers, and the copies agree at first, then slowly drift apart — tomorrow they still match; by the weekend they fan out. The “70% chance of rain” is not a mood, it is a count: of all the skies the machine tried, seven in ten brought the rain.

door.q: Forty skies, one rule — the walk of simulated worlds
Forty skies to compute — who shares the machine among them?

part.name: the race
part.line: a forecast must arrive before the weather does
part.blurb: All of this is run against a deadline. If the machine needed six hours to tell you about the next six hours, the forecast would be a history lesson; the model is cut and trimmed until tomorrow fits inside a couple of hours, and the answer must then cross the wires to your pocket before the first drop falls. Speed, here, is not a convenience. It is the difference between a warning and a report.

door.q: Who gives the beat, and who goes next?
The answer must cross the wire before the rain does

card.bottom: Readings, cells, sums, and a picture: tomorrow is the deck’s oldest trick — the world measured into numbers, a program walking them forward, and the answer painted back. The trails below open each step of the trick; at their ends, the primers are waiting.

door.q: The trail that ends at a real machine
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Finding where you are
card.q: How does your phone know where it is?

part.name: the four whispers
part.line: the sky, talking and never listening
part.blurb: Somewhere above you, a machine is falling around the Earth and shouting where it is and what time it is. Your phone hears four of these whispers and answers nothing: it never speaks back; it only listens. Four is not a whim — three whispers narrow the dot to one place, and the fourth is for the phone’s own cheap clock, so the sum can come out right.

door.q: The machines doing the shouting — the trail of the machines themselves
A message chopped, numbered, and kept until received

part.name: the blue dot
part.line: your position, painted onto a picture of numbers
part.blurb: The fix arrives as numbers, and what you see is a dot on a map. The map is not a rolled-up photograph: to the phone it is a list of corners and edges with lengths, painted as a picture only when you look. The blue dot is three numbers wearing a halo of honesty — the little circle around it is the machine admitting how unsure it is, and the halo is drawn, too, from arithmetic.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
A dot wants a route — how a route finds its way

part.name: the solve
part.line: four distances, one point, arithmetic to the rescue
part.blurb: Each whisper tells the phone how long it travelled: light crosses about three hundred metres in a millionth of a second, so the delay becomes a distance. Four distances mean four spheres that must meet in one place — you. The phone solves it by walking: guess a point, see how wrong the guess is, step toward less wrong, and repeat until the answer stops moving. Then it does it again, and again, while you walk to the corner shop.

door.q: Stepping toward the answer until it stops moving — a recipe that contains a copy of itself
The arithmetic, walked by a machine — what the machine is

part.name: the roads
part.line: the city, spelled as corners and edges
part.blurb: Between fixes, the dot must keep walking: the phone guesses where you have moved and snaps the guess to the likeliest road — a search through facts (these edges, these lengths, these one-way streets) for the path that best explains the numbers. This is why the dot sometimes slides along a fence: the roads in the machine are not the roads in the world, and the search only knows the numbers it was given.

door.q: Roads as facts, walked to the likeliest answer
The likeliest path, found by a recipe that contains a copy of itself

part.name: the receiver
part.line: a machine in your pocket, listening to the sky
part.blurb: The listener is a chip smaller than your thumbnail. It strains the whispers out of noise far louder than they are, and hands the phone numbers to walk; the trick of hearing a whisper below the noise is old and clever, and the chip doing it is the same design as everything else in the phone: fetch, decode, execute, one more costume on the one machine.

door.q: The one design, in every box — even this one
The faintest song: a whisper measured out of noise

part.name: the assist
part.line: the wire lending a hand to the sky
part.blurb: A phone that knows nothing must find satellites blind — listening for whispers it cannot name, which takes minutes. So the phone cheats, politely: over the wire it downloads the sky’s timetable, which machines are overhead and roughly where, and the fix arrives in seconds instead. Your phone and the sky work together every time the dot appears, one feeding the other the numbers it needs, just in time.

door.q: The timetable, poured over the wire, just in time
One receiver, every app that wants a fix — who shares it?

part.name: the clock
part.line: the whole trick is a clock race
part.blurb: Distances from delays stand or fall on time, and not roughly: a millionth of a second is three hundred metres, so the satellites carry atomic clocks, tended from the ground. Even Einstein gets a correction in — the satellites move fast enough, and sit far enough from the Earth’s pull, that time ticks differently for them, and the sky’s clocks are wound back to match ours, daily, on purpose. Positioning is not a map service that happens to use clocks. It is clocks, wearing a map.

door.q: What is a clock, that its ticks can be counted on?
Who keeps the satellite’s clock honest?

card.bottom: Whispers, ticks, sums, roads: the blue dot is arithmetic on time, all the way down. The trails below open each step; at their ends, the primers are waiting.

door.q: The trail of the machines that whisper
The trail that ends at a real machine

card.title: Getting to orbit
card.q: How do you put a machine in the sky and make it stay?

part.name: the senses
part.line: a stubborn wheel that feels every tilt
part.blurb: A rocket must know its own lean, and the classic answer is a wheel: spin it fast and it keeps its direction, stubbornly, the way a bicycle wheel resists a sideways shove. Ask the wheel which way it points now and it tells you. Small weights on springs feel the shove of the engines. Every answer is rounded to a number. The machine never feels the sky. It reads a column of numbers about itself, and steers on them.

door.q: Glass, buttons, spinning wheels: what does a machine feel of the world?
A lean past a limit is a yes-or-no fork

part.name: the count
part.line: T-minus: a list of instructions, read out by a machine
part.blurb: A launch is a list, written down in advance: chill the fuel, pressurise, light, check the numbers, let go of the clamps. A program walks the list, and when a reading is wrong it holds — the hold is not a failure but a pause in the list, a fork taken honestly. Nothing on the pad is done by someone feeling brave. It is instructions, obeyed exactly, in the oldest arrangement there is.

door.q: What does following the list mean, exactly?
Every hold is an honest fork

part.name: the guidance
part.line: steered toward a speed, not a place
part.blurb: The aim is not a point in the sky but a sideways speed: the machine is steered, thousands of times a second, toward the fall that misses. The steering is arithmetic on the senses (where am I, which way, how fast) against a plan computed in advance, and the plan walks forward, one small step after another, until the numbers agree. The rocket does not know what an orbit is. It makes the numbers match, and the fall happens.

door.q: A path computed in advance and walked step by step
Who runs the steering while the fire is lit?
A flight walked on the ground before it is flown — the trail of simulated worlds

part.name: the engines
part.line: a fire held steady by plumbing and a clock
part.blurb: A rocket pushes against nothing — not the air, only its own exhaust. Throw mass out of the back hard enough and the machine is shoved forward. That is the whole engine, and everything else is plumbing holding the fire steady: pumps drinking rivers, valves that open in order, walls that would melt if the cold fuel did not stream along them. Nine tenths of the machine is fuel; the empty tanks are let go mid-sky, because hauling emptiness is wasted fire.

door.q: The machine in every box, at its angriest
A vocabulary small enough for a valve: light, throttle, stop
A number opens a valve — how does a number push?

part.name: the beat
part.line: valves on a beat of milliseconds
part.blurb: Inside, the fury is a dance on a clock: this valve now, that measurement next, ignition on this beat, throttle on that — a controller walking its round, the same fetch, decode, execute as the phone in your pocket, wearing a fireproof coat. When the shake is worst and the noise is total, what holds the machine together is the oldest thing in it: a list, walked exactly, on time.

door.q: The dance — fetch, decode, execute
Who keeps the beat when everything shakes?

part.name: the vote
part.line: three computers, one answer
part.blurb: When the stakes are a machine’s whole existence, one yes-or-no is not enough: three computers read the same numbers and vote on every step, and when they disagree the vote decides — or the vote says stop. An abort is not a failure but a fork taken honestly, priced in advance; losing a machine is cheaper than losing everything it was carrying. The whole ascent is a braid of small questions answered together, in time.

door.q: Three writers, one answer — the honest ways of agreeing
The vocabulary of yes and no — and of maybe, by voting

part.name: the window
part.line: the moment the sky passes over the pad
part.blurb: A target orbit is a plane through the planet, and it passes over the launch pad at a calculable instant: miss the window and you wait for the Earth to bring it round again — sometimes a day, sometimes weeks, for the rare roads between planets. The last seconds of the count guard the whole month: one moment is worth everything, and the moment itself was computed, like everything else on the pad, in advance, from numbers.

door.q: The window hands the machine to the sky — the trail of what it does up there
Every number watched from the ground, over the wire

card.bottom: Senses, lists, arithmetic, fire, forks: the rocket is the whole deck in one afternoon: the world read as numbers, a program walking them, a machine obeying, forks that can say no, all to hand one sealed computer to the sky, where it falls forever and never lands.

door.q: The trail of the machine in the sky
The trail that ends at a real machine

card.title: Talking to a machine
card.q: Where do its words come from, when nobody wrote them?

part.name: the words at the door
part.line: your sentence, cut into pieces and measured
part.blurb: You type a sentence, and the machine never sees it. First it cuts the text into pieces, usually shorter than words, and turns each piece into a list of numbers: a point in a space of thousands of dimensions, where words used alike sit close together. “King” and “queen” are neighbours there, and so are “dog” and “puppy”. Everything you wrote is geometry before the machine begins.

door.q: How does a word become a place?
How small can a language made for a machine be?

part.name: the next word
part.line: a probability for every word it knows, one picked, then again
part.blurb: Everything it ever does is one thing: given the words so far, guess the next one. It scores every word it knows (a probability for “the”, a probability for “tomorrow”, for each of tens of thousands of others), picks one, appends it, and starts again. The paragraph it hands you is a chain of such picks. Nobody wrote the paragraph; it assembled itself, one likely word at a time.

door.q: A fork made of probabilities — what is deciding made of?
It holds a model of language — what is a model?

part.name: the school
part.line: guesses scored, every knob nudged toward the better guess
part.blurb: Nobody taught it rules of grammar. It was shown oceans of text and corrected: guess the next word, compare with what really came, and let the error flow backwards through the network, nudging billions of internal knobs a hair toward the answer that would have been right. Repeat a trillion times, and the guesses stop being noise and start being language. Nobody wrote the guesses; they were grown.

door.q: How a machine improves its guesses
The other way down: software that is written, not learned

part.name: the engine
part.line: immense grids of numbers multiplied, all at once
part.blurb: All of it, the geometry and the guessing and the scoring, is arithmetic: enormous grids of numbers multiplied together. A processor does its sums one after another, which would take years. But the chips built to paint games, thousands of small painters working side by side, turn out to be exactly the machine for grids of numbers. The painters were rehired; the engines of guessing are game chips that learned math.

door.q: How a game chip learned math
The painting it was born for — the thousand small painters

part.name: the context
part.line: the conversation so far, held and re-read with every word
part.blurb: It seems to remember you. What it holds is the conversation so far — your words and its own, kept in memory and fed back in with every guess. There is a limit to what fits, and when the early words fall out of that held window they are not forgotten the way you forget; they are evicted. The machine that knows your whole history has re-read it all. The machine in this window has not.

door.q: How does a circuit hold the words so far?
Who keeps the words and the turns in order?

part.name: the room behind the answer
part.line: a warehouse of machines, acting as one, at the end of a wire
part.blurb: The reply seems to come from nowhere in particular. It comes from a warehouse: racks of machines far away, many machines acting as one, trading your words over the wire. The voice has no single place you could point to — it is a building wearing a conversation, and the wire is the whole of where it lives.

door.q: How many machines act as one
How the words cross the wire

part.name: the confident mistake
part.line: fluency without facts, when the facts were never learned
part.blurb: Because its words are guesses, not lookups, it can be wrong in a way no encyclopedia can: fluently, in perfect grammar, citing a paper that does not exist. The fluency is real, the words really do fit together, and the facts are optional. The cure is the oldest one in computing: make the machine look things up instead of guessing. What cannot be cured is the confidence; that is how it was built.

door.q: What looking the answer up, instead of guessing it, would look like
Where the better guesses come from
What is a thought, that a machine could have one?

card.bottom: Clarke said any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, and advanced is the operative word: past your understanding, and it reads as magic. The two words are cousins — magic and mechanism trace back to one ancient root that simply meant power. Follow any part of this trail down and the power dissolves into arithmetic, done very fast by very dumb switches. The trails below lead the rest of the way; at their ends, the primers are waiting.

door.q: How a machine improves its guesses — the hinge this card turns on
The trail of the model — how a world is simulated
